title: Maximal Square
description: Brute force to optimized: growing and validating candidate squares directly versus a 2D DP recurrence based on the minimum of 3 neighboring values.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an m x n binary matrix filled with '0' and '1' characters, find the largest SQUARE containing only '1's, and return its area.

blocks.caption: Each cell's largest ending square depends on the minimum of its top, left, and top-left neighbors

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An m x n binary character matrix"],["Output","The area (side length squared) of the largest all-1s SQUARE"],["Goal","Find this efficiently, without checking every possible square directly"],["Constraints","m == matrix.length; n == matrix[i].length; 1 <= m, n <= 300; matrix[i][j] is '0' or '1'"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Looking for the largest all-1s SQUARE (not a general rectangle)","The restriction to squares (equal width and height) enables a much simpler DP recurrence than the general rectangle case"],["A square ending at a given cell depends on smaller squares ending at its neighbors","Define dp[i][j] as the side length of the largest square with its bottom-right corner at (i,j)"],["A larger square can only exist if its top, left, AND top-left neighboring squares are all at least as large","dp[i][j] is limited by the SMALLEST (the bottleneck) of those three neighboring values, plus one"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a binary matrix, find the largest square (equal side lengths) consisting entirely of '1' cells, and return its area.

blocks.title: Analogy: Growing the Biggest Possible Square Tile From Existing Smaller Ones
blocks.text: Like tiling a floor with square tiles of varying sizes already placed, and figuring out the biggest NEW square tile that could be placed with its bottom-right corner at a specific spot. That new tile can only be as large as the smallest of the three existing tiles directly above, directly to the left, and diagonally above-left of it, plus one more unit, since all three of those directions must support the new tile's full width and height.

blocks.caption: A square growing to size k at (i,j) requires squares of at least size k-1 at all three neighboring directions

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: matrix with a well-known largest-square answer

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["A 2x2 block of all-1s cells exists (for example, around rows 2-3, columns 3-4)","Largest square side length: 2","This is the biggest square achievable anywhere in this matrix"],["Answer","4","Side length 2, squared, gives an area of 4"]]}

blocks.text: Example: matrix = [[0,1],[1,0]]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["No two adjacent 1s ever align to form even a 2x2 square","Largest square side length: 1","Only single, isolated 1 cells exist, each forming a trivial 1x1 square"],["Answer","1","Side length 1, squared, gives an area of 1"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?
Before checking every possible square size at every possible position directly, notice that a square's achievable size at any position depends only on 3 specific neighboring positions.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Define dp[i][j] as the side length of the largest all-1s square whose BOTTOM-RIGHT corner is exactly at (i, j).

Observation 2: If matrix[i][j] is '0', no square can possibly end here, so dp[i][j] = 0.

Observation 3: If matrix[i][j] is '1', the largest square ending here extends the smallest of the three neighboring squares (directly above, directly left, and diagonally above-left) by exactly one more row and column, since a bigger square requires ALL THREE of those neighboring directions to already support it.

Observation 4: So dp[i][j] = min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) + 1 when the current cell is '1'. Track the maximum dp value seen anywhere, and the answer is that maximum, squared.

Recognizing that a square (unlike a general rectangle) only depends on 3 specific neighboring DP values, rather than needing an entire histogram-and-monotonic-stack machinery, is what makes this simpler recurrence possible.

This is a 2D DP problem where each cell's value depends on the minimum of 3 specific neighbors (top, left, top-left), a much simpler recurrence than the general "largest rectangle" problem, made possible specifically because squares have equal width and height.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every '1' cell, try growing a square from it as far as possible, checking each new row and column directly.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every cell that is '1', treat it as a potential top-left corner and try growing a square of increasing size.
At each size increase, check whether the newly added bottom row and right column (needed to grow the square by one) are entirely '1's; stop growing the moment this fails.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Growing starts from every '1' cell independently, since this brute force does not yet share work between overlapping square checks.
Only the NEWLY added row and column need checking at each growth step, since the interior was already validated by the previous, smaller square.
The growth stops immediately once a check fails, since a larger square built from this same corner could never succeed either.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible square, grown from every possible starting corner, is checked directly, so the correct maximum side length is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols * min(rows, cols)) in the worst case, since each of the rows*cols starting positions can grow up to min(rows,cols) times, each growth check costing O(side).
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: growing and validating a square from every possible starting position independently ignores that the achievable square size at any position can be derived directly from just 3 already-computed neighboring values.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force independently grows and validates a square from every starting position. Instead, build a DP table where dp[i][j] represents the side length of the largest square ending exactly at (i,j). Fill it in a single pass: if the current cell is '1', dp[i][j] = min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) + 1; if it's '0', dp[i][j] = 0. Track the maximum dp value seen, and return its square as the final answer.

Build a (rows+1) by (cols+1) table, initialized to 0. For each cell (i, j) from 1 to rows and 1 to cols, if matrix[i-1][j-1] is '1', set dp[i][j] to the minimum of dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], and dp[i-1][j-1], plus 1, updating the running maximum. Return the maximum squared.
9. Optimized Solution
Fill a DP table where each cell's value is derived directly from 3 specific neighboring values.
Dry run: resulting DP table (matrix from the earlier example, 1-indexed, row/col 0 are the padding border)

blocks.title: Reading the table
blocks.text: The largest value anywhere in the table is 2, found at (i=3,j=4) and (i=3,j=5), meaning a 2x2 all-1s square ends at each of those positions. The final answer is 2 squared = 4, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), filling every DP cell exactly once with O(1) work.
Space: O(rows * cols) for the table (reducible to O(cols) using a rolling row, since each row only depends on the row directly above it).
Why This Works

A square of side k ending at (i,j) requires that the (k-1)-sided squares ending at (i-1,j) (above), (i,j-1) (left), and (i-1,j-1) (diagonally above-left) all already exist, since together they cover every cell of the larger square except its own new bottom row and right column (which are guaranteed '1' by the current cell being '1' and the recurrence's construction). Taking the MINIMUM of those three ensures the new square is only as large as its most constrained direction allows.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["matrix[i-1][j-1] == '1'","dp[i][j] extends the smallest neighboring square by exactly one"],["matrix[i-1][j-1] == '0'","dp[i][j] = 0, since no square can possibly end at a '0' cell"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The DP table is sized (rows+1) by (cols+1) so row 0 and column 0 naturally represent "no square possible", always holding 0.
The min-of-three-plus-one recurrence is applied only when the current cell is '1'; otherwise the default 0 is left in place.
maxSide is updated inline as the table is filled, avoiding a separate final scan over the whole table.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (grow and validate from every corner)","O(rows * cols * min(rows,cols))","O(1) extra","Each starting position independently grows and validates its own candidate square"],["Optimized (2D DP, min-of-three-neighbors recurrence)","O(rows * cols)","O(rows * cols)","Each cell is filled exactly once using 3 already-computed neighboring values"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Restricting the general "largest rectangle" problem to SQUARES specifically enables a much simpler DP recurrence (depending on just 3 neighbors), avoiding the need for a monotonic stack or histogram machinery.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to take the MINIMUM of the three neighboring values, and instead using just one of them (e.g., only the top or only the left), which would incorrectly ignore a constraining direction.
Returning the maximum side length directly instead of squaring it, forgetting the problem asks for AREA, not side length.
Confusing this problem with Maximal Rectangle, and applying the more complex histogram-based technique unnecessarily when the simpler DP recurrence suffices here.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["matrix has no '1' cells at all","The answer is 0, since every dp cell stays 0"],["matrix is entirely '1's","The answer is min(rows, cols) squared, the largest square that fits within the matrix's dimensions"],["matrix has only 1 row or 1 column","The largest achievable square has side length at most 1 (any isolated 1 forms a valid 1x1 square)"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly justify WHY the minimum of the three neighbors is the correct constraint (all three directions must support the new, larger square simultaneously), since this justification is exactly what separates a well-reasoned DP recurrence from a guessed one.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Largest all-1s SQUARE (not rectangle) in a binary matrix" points toward a 2D DP recurrence based on the minimum of the top, left, and top-left neighboring DP values, plus one.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you reduce the space usage? Since each row only depends on the row directly above it, a rolling 1D array of size (cols+1) suffices, reducing space to O(cols).

How does this differ from Maximal Rectangle? That problem allows any width/height combination (not just equal), requiring the more general histogram-and-monotonic-stack technique instead of this simpler 3-neighbor DP recurrence.

How would you also report the actual square's location, not just its area? Track the (row, column) position where the maximum dp value was found; the square then spans from (row - maxSide + 1, column - maxSide + 1) to (row, column).

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A simpler, more constrained sibling of Maximal Rectangle elsewhere in this category, restricted specifically to squares, enabling a direct 3-neighbor DP recurrence instead of the histogram/monotonic-stack approach that problem requires.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(rows * cols * min(rows,cols)) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (2D DP, min-of-three-neighbors): O(rows * cols) time, O(rows * cols) space (reducible to O(cols)).
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: 2D DP where each cell's value is the minimum of its top, left, and top-left neighbors, plus one
Core Idea: A square of side k ending at (i,j) requires (k-1)-sided squares at all three neighboring directions; the achievable size is bounded by whichever is smallest
Time: O(rows * cols)
Space: O(rows * cols), reducible to O(cols)
Most Important Observation: Restricting to squares (equal width and height) enables a much simpler DP recurrence than the general largest-rectangle problem
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: dp[i][j] = min(top, left, top-left) + 1 if '1', else 0; answer is (max dp)^2
